findings.claim: 40 of the 48 practice questions are labelled “20 marks — Extract Analysis”; the other 8 are labelled “40 marks — 19th Century Essay”.
findings.truth: Section B of the 2 hour 30 minute paper is ONE source-based question worth 40 marks, with an extract printed. All 48 relabelled “40 marks — Extract Analysis”.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md 2.2: ‘Section B (20%) 19th Century Prose (40 marks) … through a source based response’.

findings.claim: Mark ladders read “Top band (9–10) … Lower band (1–2)” or “Top band (4–5) … Lower band (1)”.
findings.truth: Ladders were scaled to 20 or to 10/5 marks. Rescaled to the five house bands over 40: Top 33–40, Upper-mid 25–32, Mid 17–24, Lower-mid 9–16, Low 1–8.
findings.evidence: House ladder used by the sibling Eduqas units (jane-eyre, pride-and-prejudice).

findings.claim: Ten mark schemes end “AO4 (up to 10): Accurate expression.” and split the 40 marks equally over four objectives.
findings.truth: The 19th-century prose question assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3 only. AO4 is assessed in Section A of this paper, not here, and the spec publishes no per-objective mark split for the section. The AO4 line is removed and the guidance folded into the top band.
findings.evidence: Spec 2.2: ‘Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3.’

findings.claim: The board is named in 14 student-facing places, e.g. “For the Eduqas C720U Component 2 Section B exam” (L1), “If your Eduqas extract” (L2), the L8 description, a knowledge-check stem and a flashcard.
findings.truth: House rule: Eduqas lessons never name the board, the spec code or the section code in student-facing text. All reworded to “the exam” / “the 19th-century novel question”.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT banned-string list; neutral-phrasing house rule.

findings.claim: “Context (AO3) is worth up to 10 of the 40 marks.”
findings.truth: The spec gives no per-objective mark split for this section. The figure is not sourced and is almost certainly low: AO3 is 7.5% of the qualification in this component, and this is the only section of it that assesses AO3, which works out at 15 of the 40 marks. The false figure is removed rather than replaced.
findings.evidence: Spec 3.1 weighting table: Component 2 AO3 = 7.5%; Sections A and C assess no AO3.

findings.claim: “Before we judge [the Martians] too harshly, we must remember …”, repeated in a mark scheme as ‘before we judge them too harshly’.
findings.truth: Wells writes ‘And before we judge of them too harshly we must remember’ — no comma, and ‘judge of them’.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg text, Book One ch.1.

findings.claim: Twice: ‘his mind kept returning to “the normal”’.
findings.truth: The word ‘normal’ does not appear anywhere in the novel. Presented as a quotation, it is fabricated. Quotation marks removed; the surrounding claim (he expected a shell in the pit to finish them) is sound.
findings.evidence: grep -i 'normal' over the full text returns no hit; Book One ch.7: ‘A shell in the pit … will kill them all.’

findings.claim: “People bring picnic hampers.”
findings.truth: No hampers in the crowd scene. Wells lists carriages, ‘quite a heap of bicycles’ and a sweet-stuff dealer’s barrow of green apples and ginger beer.
findings.evidence: Book One ch.5.

findings.claim: ‘The narrator observes that “the social order” dissolves’.
findings.truth: Not a contiguous quotation — the text has ‘the commonplace habits of our social order’ and ‘topple that social order headlong’. Quotation marks removed.
findings.evidence: Book One ch.8.

findings.claim: The glossary pop-up on ‘first-person narrator’ reads “A narrator whose account cannot be fully trusted …”.
findings.truth: That is the definition of an unreliable narrator. A student taught this would misuse the term. Replaced with the correct definition; the lesson’s own glossary already had it right.
findings.evidence: Same lesson, GLOSSARY_TERMS entry ‘first-person narrator’.

findings.claim: “monstrous tripods, higher than many houses, striding over the young pine trees.”
findings.truth: Wells’s sentence is singular: ‘A monstrous tripod, higher than many houses, striding over the young pine trees’.
findings.evidence: Book One ch.10.

findings.claim: Tripods are ‘over a hundred feet tall’ / ‘over 100 feet’ in the text, a pop-up, a flashcard, the glossary and a knowledge-check option.
findings.truth: The novel says ‘nearly a hundred feet’ and ‘a hundred feet high’. Changed to ‘about’ throughout, including the knowledge-check option (answer index unchanged).
findings.evidence: Book One ch.14 and Book Two ch.7.

findings.claim: “It manages to destroy one tripod before being sunk”, “the Thunder Child destroys one tripod but is then overwhelmed”, and a flashcard saying the same.
findings.truth: The Thunder Child kills TWO Martians — one cut down by gunfire, then a second crushed by the burning wreck. The captain shouts ‘Two!’ A student writing ‘one’ loses the point about the cost of the victory.
findings.evidence: Book One ch.17.

findings.claim: “The tripods emit a chilling ‘ulla, ulla’ cry that haunts the narrator throughout the novel.”
findings.truth: ‘Ulla, ulla, ulla, ulla’ is heard only in Book Two ch.8, and it is the wail of the last dying Martian, not a tripod cry running through the book. The fighting machines howl ‘Aloo! Aloo!’ Both restored to their real places.
findings.evidence: Book One ch.10 (Aloo) and Book Two ch.8 (Dead London).

findings.claim: The curate ‘wails “What are these Martians? … What has God wrought?”’.
findings.truth: ‘What has God wrought?’ is not in the novel. The curate says ‘Why are these things permitted? What sins have we done?’ and ‘What are these Martians?’
findings.evidence: Book One ch.13; ‘wrought’ appears in the text only in ch.1 and ch.6 of Book Two.

findings.claim: “slain by the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this earth.”, and a knowledge-check stem quoting it without ‘in his wisdom’.
findings.truth: Not contiguous. Wells writes ‘slain, after all man’s devices had failed, by the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this earth’. Restored in both places.
findings.evidence: Book Two ch.8.

findings.claim: The artilleryman selects the “strong and sane” (L4 content, L5 content) and a L5 flashcard gives ‘Strong and sane’ as the phrase for the NARRATOR’s state before the invasion.
findings.truth: ‘Strong and sane’ appears nowhere in the novel. The artilleryman’s phrase is ‘able-bodied, clean-minded men’. The flashcard also misattributed the artilleryman’s idea to the narrator; it now asks for the narrator’s own self-description.
findings.evidence: Book Two ch.7.

findings.claim: The epilogue is quoted as “We can never regard this earth as the entire universe, or regard any creature of its own in the same way we did before.” (L4), and the same invented line drives a L7 paragraph, a L7 knowledge-check stem, two L7 flashcards and a L7 mark scheme.
findings.truth: Fabricated. Wells writes ‘We have learned now that we cannot regard this planet as being fenced in and a secure abiding place for Man’. Six places corrected; the knowledge-check answer index is unchanged.
findings.evidence: The Epilogue.

findings.claim: The narrator is a “professed student of philosophy”.
findings.truth: He calls himself ‘a professed and recognised writer on philosophical themes’ (and, in the epilogue, says his province is speculative philosophy).
findings.evidence: Book Two ch.7 and the Epilogue.

findings.claim: “The narrator says ‘I did not know then what I know now’.”
findings.truth: Not in the novel. Replaced with Wells’s real retrospective phrase, ‘those departed days’, which makes the same point.
findings.evidence: Book One ch.1.

findings.claim: Direct address is illustrated with “the reader will remember”.
findings.truth: Not in the novel. Wells writes ‘I scarcely need remind the reader’.
findings.evidence: Book One ch.1.

findings.claim: The Martians have “atrophied digestive systems”.
findings.truth: They have none: ‘Entrails they had none. They did not eat, much less digest.’ Lesson 5 states this correctly, so the unit contradicted itself.
findings.evidence: Book Two ch.2.

findings.claim: Lesson 8 teaches AO4 throughout: a whole section headed “AO4: Quality of Expression”, “Where written accuracy is assessed, careless spelling, punctuation, and grammar will cost you marks”, a takeaway reading “40 marks split equally across AO1, AO2, AO3, AO4”, an AO-matching knowledge check pairing AO4 with ‘Accuracy of expression’, a flashcard on what AO4 rewards, and a glossary entry tagging proofreading (AO4).
findings.truth: This question assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3 (context) only. Spelling, punctuation and grammar earn no marks on the 19th-century prose question, and the 40 marks are not split equally over four objectives. Eleven text edits plus the knowledge check, flashcard and glossary corrected; the AO-match item now pairs AO3 with context.
findings.evidence: Spec 2.2: ‘Section B assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3.’ AO4 sits in Section A of the same paper.

findings.claim: Wells is called ‘an atheist’ in L4 and L5 content and in a mark scheme.
findings.truth: Defensible but not certain: Wells left Christianity young, yet published God the Invisible King (1917) arguing for a finite God before repudiating it. ‘A lifelong critic of organised religion’ would be safer. Not edited — it is not mark-affecting and the sentence works either way.
findings.evidence: Wells, Experiment in Autobiography (1934); God the Invisible King (1917).

findings.claim: “Wells was also a committed socialist, a member of the Fabian Society alongside George Bernard Shaw.”
findings.truth: True of Wells, but he joined the Fabian Society in 1903, five years after the novel. The paragraph is about the novel’s composition, so a reader could take it as 1898 context. Not edited — the sentence makes no date claim.
findings.evidence: Standard Wells biography; Fabian membership 1903–1908.

findings.claim: Should the unit state a mark figure for context on this question?
findings.truth: Two options. (a) Say nothing, as edited now — safe, because the spec publishes no per-objective split for the section. (b) State ‘context is worth 15 of the 40 marks’, which follows from the weighting table: Component 2 carries 120 marks, AO3 is 7.5% of the 200-mark qualification in this component, and Section B is the only section of the paper that assesses AO3. Recommendation: (a) unless a published mark scheme confirms 15, since a wrong number is worse than none.
findings.evidence: Spec 3.1 weighting table plus the per-section AO statements in 2.2.

summary: Lesson 8 carried the exam damage: it taught AO4 and SPaG marks on a question that assesses AO1, AO2 and AO3 only, and claimed the 40 marks split equally over four objectives. Seven fabricated or misquoted lines were found — the invented epilogue quotation used in six places across L4 and L7, the curate’s ‘What has God wrought?’, the artilleryman’s ‘strong and sane’ (also given to the narrator on a flashcard), ‘the normal’, ‘professed student of philosophy’ and ‘I did not know then what I know now’. The one plot error is L3: the Thunder Child kills two Martians, not one. Fleet-wide, all 48 practice questions were mislabelled and 14 places named the board.
